claims.text: The magnetocaloric response and hysteresis are governed by the nanoscale spatial distribution and size of magnetically active ordered domains.
The magnetically active ordered domains have a hexagonal structure.
The ordered hexagonal domains occur within a predominantly disordered matrix.
Mild post-deposition annealing can tune the ordered-domain size and spatial distribution.
The as-deposited FeMnNiGeSi alloy consists of a single ordered hexagonal phase.
The as-deposited alloy undergoes a sharp first-order magnetostructural transition.
The as-deposited transition produces a large but hysteretic entropy change.
The as-deposited material has limited heat-exchange rates because of its low surface-to-volume ratio.
Low-temperature, short-duration annealing below the transition temperature will induce nanoscale heterogeneity in chemical or structural ordering without causing phase decomposition.
The relevant structural mediators are ordered-domain size, domain distribution, and interfacial strain.
Low-temperature annealing produces smaller or more finely distributed hexagonal domains.
Smaller or more finely distributed domains reduce the energetic barrier for the magnetostructural transition and thereby lower hysteresis.
The annealed domain structure maintains a sizable but less abrupt magnetocaloric entropy change.
Greater interfacial area between ordered and disordered regions facilitates a smoother transformation under low applied fields.
Annealing will broaden the magnetic-entropy-change peak while slightly reducing its peak magnitude relative to the as-deposited baseline.
Annealing will markedly reduce the magnetic hysteresis-loop area during low-field cooling cycles.
The annealed microstructure will improve effective heat exchange through a higher surface-to-volume microstructural feature.
Substantial composition changes or processing that induces large-scale phase separation may alter the predicted effects.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis describes ordered hexagonal domains embedded in a predominantly disordered matrix, whereas the stated as-deposited initial state is a single ordered hexagonal phase. These are incompatible descriptions unless the single-phase statement refers only to average crystallographic phase identity, which is not clarified.

The baseline heat-exchange limitation is attributed to low specimen surface-to-volume ratio, but the predicted improvement is attributed to increased internal microstructural interfacial area. Internal domain-interface area does not directly resolve low external surface-to-volume ratio, and no link between the two measures is supplied.
